draft.title: The Meiji Restoration
card: In 1868 a group of samurai leaders overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate, the military government that had ruled Japan for over 250 years. They put the young Emperor Meiji at the centre of government. This is called the Meiji Restoration.
Japan's leaders had seen how Western powers forced it to open its ports. They feared Japan could be weak against them. Their aim was to make Japan strong and wealthy enough to stand up to the West.

The new government built railways, telegraph lines and factories. It set up schools for children across the country. It also created a modern army with conscription, which meant men could be called up to serve, not just samurai.
The government copied ideas from Western countries and sent officials abroad to study them. Japan changed very quickly in a few decades.
draft.remember: Meiji leaders modernised Japan on Western models to make it strong against the West.

a.q: Why did the Meiji government copy Western railways, factories and armies?
opts: To make Japan strong enough to resist Western powers
To hand control of Japan to Western governments
To bring back the rule of the Tokugawa shogun
To end the emperor's role in Japanese government
a.why: The leaders had seen Western powers force Japan to open its ports, so they wanted a strong, wealthy country. Copying Western methods was a way to gain that strength, not a way to give up control to the West.
a.clue: Think about what the leaders feared after the ports were opened.

b.q: Which change shows how the Meiji government built a modern army?
opts: Calling up men for service, not only samurai
Allowing only samurai to serve as soldiers
Hiring foreign armies to defend Japan
Closing Japan's ports to all foreign ships
b.why: Conscription meant men from many backgrounds could be called up to serve. Before this, fighting was the work of the samurai class, which is why limiting service to samurai describes the old system, not the new one.
b.clue: The modern army was not just for one class.

a.best: To make Japan strong enough to resist Western powers

b.best: Calling up men for service, not only samurai
